title: Monic reduction forces monicity for a commuting idempotent determinant
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $I\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(A)$ an ideal, and $T,P\in\operatorname{Mat}_J(A)$ for a finite set $J$. Assume $P^2=P$, $TP=PT$, and the reduction of $D(T,P)$ [def-weil-pbc-idempotent-charpoly] in $(A/I)[X]$ is monic. Then $D(T,P)$ is monic.

source.place: Tag 09XI, lemma-characterize-henselian-pair, proof of (3) implies (1), splitting and characteristic-polynomial paragraphs; matrix formula and omitted details written out by G2

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-idempotent-charpoly-leading-coeff] to get c*c=c for c=leadingCoeff D(T,P). Treat the zero ring directly. Otherwise I is proper since it is contained in the Jacobson radical, so A/I is nonzero.

An idempotent e with image zero in A/I lies in I and hence in the Jacobson radical. The element 1-e is a unit by the Jacobson characterization, and (1-e)*e=0, so e=0. If the image of c were zero, c would be zero and D(T,P) would be zero, contradicting monicity of its reduction over the nonzero ring A/I. Thus c survives reduction.

Because c survives reduction, the leading coefficient of the mapped polynomial is the image of c. Monicity of the reduction gives that image equal to 1. The element 1-c is idempotent and maps to zero; the preceding idempotent argument gives 1-c=0. Hence c=1 and D(T,P) is monic.
